A.explanation: Both p.d. and e.m.f. are energy transferred per unit charge, so both are $W/q$ with unit volt equal to joule per coulomb.

B.explanation: p.d. is correctly $W/q$, but e.m.f. is also energy per unit charge, not $Wq$ which has units $\text{J C}$.

C.explanation: e.m.f. is correctly $W/q$, but p.d. is also energy per unit charge, not $Wq$.

D.explanation: Neither quantity is $Wq$ because multiplying energy $W$ by charge $q$ does not give energy per unit charge or the volt.

hints: Notice the question asks for energy transfer $W$ in joules and charge $q$ in coulombs, while both p.d. and e.m.f. are measured in volts.
Recall that one volt is one joule per coulomb, so look for the combination of $W$ and $q$ that gives $\text{J C}^{-1}$.

Compare the direction of energy transfer: p.d. is energy lost per unit charge in a component and e.m.f. is energy gained per unit charge from a source, but check whether that changes the $W$ and $q$ mathematics.
walkthrough: Identify what is given: energy transfer $W$ and charge $q$. Both p.d. across a component and e.m.f. of a source are measured in volts ($\text{V}$).
State the physical rule: p.d. is defined as the energy transferred per unit charge when charge passes through a component, so $V = W/q$.
State the parallel rule: e.m.f. is defined as the energy transferred per unit charge from chemical or other store to electrical store when charge passes through the source, so $E = W/q$.
Check units: $W/q$ has units $\text{J}/\text{C} = \text{V}$, which matches both quantities, whereas $Wq$ has units $\text{J C}$ which is not a volt.
Therefore both columns must show $W/q$. This is option A.
